method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)' (current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024), 16 claims; LICENCE: © RANZCOG. Website disclaimer: 'All aspects of this website and any phone application, including data, documents, graphics and logos are copyright to RANZCOG and may not be reproduced in any shape or form. Unless otherwise agreed by RANZCOG in writing, you are provided with access for your personal use.' (read at https://ranzcog.edu.au/disclaimer/ (section 2, Copyright and Restricted Use; the PDF itself carries no licence statement)). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Working Group for Preterm Birth (Shennan A, Suff N, Simpson JL, Jacobsson B, Mol BW, Grobman WA), International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics 155(1):16-18, doi 10.1002/ijgo.13852 'FIGO good practice recommendations on progestogens for prevention of preterm delivery' (published October 2021), 6 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC9291591). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. PDF fetched 2026-09-24 and converted with pdftotext -layout. The two recommendations sit in a two-column table whose grade column interleaves with the text, so they are anchored in pieces. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the FIGO 2021 good practice recommendations (based on the 2021 EPPPIC individual-participant meta-analysis), because the RANZCOG statement is past its review date; S1's claims and anchors are unchanged. S2 is CC BY-NC-ND and is paraphrased and hash-anchored.

claims.claim: **Preterm birth is the main cause of newborn deaths, so preventing it is a priority;** about two thirds of preterm births are spontaneous and the rest are medically indicated.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A short cervix measured by transvaginal ultrasound in mid-pregnancy strongly predicts spontaneous preterm birth.**
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Recommend vaginal progesterone to asymptomatic women whose cervix measures under 25 mm on mid-trimester transvaginal ultrasound.** (Consensus-based recommendation)
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In a cervix of 25 mm or less, vaginal progesterone lowered the rate of birth before 34 weeks to 18.1%, against 27.5% without it (RR 0.66)** in an updated meta-analysis.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **It also significantly lowered respiratory distress, composite neonatal illness or death, birth weight under 1500 g and NICU admission,** although the fall in perinatal deaths was not significant.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider progesterone for a woman with a singleton pregnancy who has previously had a spontaneous preterm singleton birth.** (Consensus-based recommendation)
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **The evidence here is mixed:** a meta-analysis of five trials favoured progesterone, but the OPPTIMUM trial (2016), which that analysis left out, found no reduction in preterm birth.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Cervical-length surveillance may pick out the women with a previous preterm birth who gain most,** and because most of these trials used intramuscular progesterone, the place of vaginal progesterone in this group is less certain.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Twins and other multiple pregnancies: routine progesterone from 24 weeks has not lowered preterm birth,** and it has not been shown to help significantly when the cervix is short, though some trials were small.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **An updated individual-patient meta-analysis in twins with a cervix of 25 mm or less found fewer births before 33 weeks with vaginal progesterone (38.5% vs 55.8%),** but RANZCOG still calls for more research to find which multiple pregnancies benefit.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Uterine malformation or 'cervical incompetence' alone: the studies are too varied and small to say whether progesterone works.** Evidence is also limited for progesterone as ongoing tocolysis after threatened preterm labour before 34 weeks.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **FIGO: offer progesterone to every woman with a singleton pregnancy at high risk,** meaning a previous spontaneous preterm birth, a short cervix on ultrasound, or both, as daily vaginal progesterone or weekly 17-OHPC. Whether it helps after a previous preterm birth when the mid-trimester cervix is longer than 30 mm is not known.
claims.locator: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Working Group for Preterm Birth (Shennan A, Suff N, Simpson JL, Jacobsson B, Mol BW, Grobman WA), International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics 155(1):16-18, doi 10.1002/ijgo.13852, 'FIGO good practice recommendations on progestogens for prevention of preterm delivery', published October 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291591/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The evidence behind it is the EPPPIC individual-participant meta-analysis (31 trials, 11 644 women):** both vaginal progesterone and 17-OHPC reduced birth before 34 weeks in high-risk singletons. Among women who qualified only through a short cervix or a previous preterm birth, the relative risk was 0.78 with vaginal progesterone (9 trials) and 0.83 with 17-OHPC (5 trials).
claims.locator: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Working Group for Preterm Birth (Shennan A, Suff N, Simpson JL, Jacobsson B, Mol BW, Grobman WA), International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics 155(1):16-18, doi 10.1002/ijgo.13852, 'FIGO good practice recommendations on progestogens for prevention of preterm delivery', published October 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291591/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **No risk factor, no progesterone:** FIGO does not recommend it for women without a previous preterm birth, a mid-trimester loss or a short cervix, because so few of them were in the trials that any benefit is unknown.
claims.locator: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Working Group for Preterm Birth (Shennan A, Suff N, Simpson JL, Jacobsson B, Mol BW, Grobman WA), International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics 155(1):16-18, doi 10.1002/ijgo.13852, 'FIGO good practice recommendations on progestogens for prevention of preterm delivery', published October 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291591/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Unselected twins or higher-order multiples: not recommended.** In EPPPIC (16 trials) neither vaginal progesterone (RR 1.01) nor 17-OHPC (RR 1.04) lowered birth before 34 weeks; for a multiple pregnancy with another risk factor, such as an earlier preterm birth, the effect is unknown.
claims.locator: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Working Group for Preterm Birth (Shennan A, Suff N, Simpson JL, Jacobsson B, Mol BW, Grobman WA), International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics 155(1):16-18, doi 10.1002/ijgo.13852, 'FIGO good practice recommendations on progestogens for prevention of preterm delivery', published October 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291591/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Either progestogen can be used, and the woman chooses with her clinician:** the only two direct comparisons found no difference between vaginal progesterone and 17-OHPC for birth before 34 weeks (RR 1.18).
claims.locator: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Working Group for Preterm Birth (Shennan A, Suff N, Simpson JL, Jacobsson B, Mol BW, Grobman WA), International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics 155(1):16-18, doi 10.1002/ijgo.13852, 'FIGO good practice recommendations on progestogens for prevention of preterm delivery', published October 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291591/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **No neurological or developmental benefit or harm has been shown in children exposed before birth:** a systematic review of 5 trials (4222 measurements in children aged 6 months to 8 years) found neither.
claims.locator: International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) Working Group for Preterm Birth (Shennan A, Suff N, Simpson JL, Jacobsson B, Mol BW, Grobman WA), International Journal of Gynecology & Obstetrics 155(1):16-18, doi 10.1002/ijgo.13852, 'FIGO good practice recommendations on progestogens for prevention of preterm delivery', published October 2021, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9291591/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **The weekly intramuscular 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate used in the US trials is not available in Australia.**
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Vaginal pessaries give high uterine levels with few systemic effects,** though vaginal irritation can be a problem. Trials used 90 mg to 400 mg and the best dose is not settled; for a short cervix, 90-100 mg and 200 mg pessaries worked equally well.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Trials began treatment as early as 16 weeks (after a previous spontaneous preterm birth) and some continued it to 37 weeks;** stopping 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone caproate early was linked to more recurrent preterm birth.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Starting progesterone at 16-24 weeks appears safe for mother and baby,** with no teratogenic effects seen, and children followed to four years in the NICHD trial showed no harm.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Long-term benefit, and the best timing, dose and route, are still unknown,** so enrolment in relevant clinical trials is encouraged.
claims.locator: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG), 'Progesterone: Use in the second and third trimester (C-Obs 29b)', current version July 2017, interim update November 2023; review due July 2024, https://ranzcog.edu.au/wp-content/uploads/Progesterone-Use-Second-Third-Trimester.pdf, retrieved 2026-09-23
